entities.name: Dafydd Gam
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Dafydd Gam, born Dafydd ap Llewelyn ap Hywel in Breconshire, Wales, rose to prominence as a fiercely loyal Welsh gentry figure in the late 14th and early 15th centuries, whose life personified the turbulent Anglo-Welsh relations during the final throes of Welsh independence movements. His unwavering opposition to Owain Glyndŵr's rebellion, a pivotal moment in Welsh history, cemented his reputation as a staunch supporter of the English Crown, ultimately leading to his death at the Battle of Agincourt on October 25, 1415. Gam's story is a microcosm of the complex loyalties and brutal realities faced by Welsh nobles caught between their national identity and the political exigencies of English dominance, making him a significant, if controversial, figure in Anglo-Welsh history.

Gam initially served King Richard II but quickly aligned himself with Henry IV following the Lancastrian usurpation in 1399, becoming a trusted retainer in the English administration of Wales. His most defining actions unfolded during the Glyndŵr Rising, which erupted in 1400. Gam consistently resisted Glyndŵr's attempts to unify Wales, famously attempting to assassinate the Welsh prince at the Welsh Parliament of Machynlleth in 1404, an act that led to his imprisonment for several years. Despite his capture, his family continued to resist Glyndŵr, holding out in their castles. Upon his release, likely around 1412, Gam rejoined the English forces, bringing his considerable martial experience to bear against the remaining Welsh rebels, solidifying his status as a key military asset.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Dafydd Gam's unwavering opposition to Owain Glyndŵr and his death at Agincourt solidified a narrative of Welsh loyalty to the English Crown, influencing Anglo-Welsh relations and military history for centuries. His actions exemplified the choices faced by Welsh gentry during a critical period of national identity formation.
